questions.stem: Water levels logged near the Aleutian Trench showed an especially small range at the Moon's quarter phase. From these measurements, which arrangement produces the largest tidal range?

options.text: Sun and Moon at right angles to Earth, so their pulls cancel partly.
Sun, Earth, and Moon aligned at new or full Moon, so their pulls reinforce.
The Moon at apogee with the Sun on the opposite side only.
A calm atmosphere with no wind-driven setup at the coast.

questions.explanation: Spring tides occur at new and full Moon when solar and lunar tides align and reinforce, producing the largest range; neap tides at the quarter phases occur when the pulls are partly opposed. Wind or the Moon's distance can modify but not define these extremes.
questions.hint: Largest range happens when the two tidal forces add together.

questions.stem: Field sketch at the Aleutian Trench notes a flat wave-cut platform exposed at low tide below a steep cliff. From these measurements, which feature is formed primarily by wave erosion cutting into a rocky coast?

options.text: A sandbar, built by deposition of sediment offshore.
A barrier island, formed by wave and wind deposition of sand.
A wave-cut platform, eroded by waves at the base of a retreating cliff.
A delta, built where a river deposits sediment into standing water.

questions.explanation: Wave erosion undercuts cliffs and leaves a flat wave-cut platform as the coast retreats, often with caves, arches, and stacks. Sandbars, barrier islands, and deltas are depositional landforms built by accumulated sediment, not carved by waves.
questions.hint: Separate features carved from rock from features built of sand.

questions.stem: Coastal survey near the Aleutian Trench records a submerged ridge of sand offshore that breaks incoming waves. From these measurements, which feature consists of a long sand ridge separated from the mainland by a lagoon?

options.text: A sea stack, an isolated remnant of an eroded headland.
A wave-cut notch, cut into the base of a cliff.
A fjord, a drowned glacial valley with steep sides.
A barrier island, built by waves and wind from accumulated sand.

questions.explanation: Barrier islands are long sandy ridges built by wave and wind deposition that run parallel to the coast and enclose a lagoon. Sea stacks and wave-cut notches are erosional rock features, and fjords are glacially carved and later flooded.
questions.hint: Sand plus a lagoon behind it points to a barrier island.

questions.stem: Gauge record at the Aleutian Trench shows a long-period sea-level pulse arriving hours after a large offshore quake. From these measurements, why does a tsunami grow dramatically as it approaches the coast?

options.text: Its speed drops in shallow water while its wavelength shortens, forcing wave height up.
It gains energy from coastal winds as it nears land.
The seafloor rises and lifts the entire ocean column uniformly.
Saltier coastal water makes the wave taller by increasing density.

questions.explanation: A tsunami travels fast with low height in the deep ocean, but as depth decreases its speed falls and its wavelength compresses; the energy flux is conserved so wave height increases dramatically. Wind, uniform uplift, and salinity do not drive this shoaling.
questions.hint: Conservation of energy as speed drops forces the wave upward.
